Notes: Year Established basis: earliest documented Judean settlement at the site = founding of the village at Khirbet Umm el-'Umdan 'in the Hellenistic period, at the end of the third or beginning of the second century BCE' (c.; midpoint -200), buildings 1 and 5 of this phase; the excavators (Onn & Weksler-Bdolah, NEAEHL vol. 5) identify the site ('lanes, buildings, a synagogue, and a mikveh') as a Jewish village, about 6 acres in extent, and suggest identifying it with the early village of Modi'in (identification disputed; rival candidates Kh. el-Hammam/el-Midya and Titura). 1 Macc 2:70 also speaks of an ancestral Hasmonean tomb at Modein, implying earlier Judean roots (undated). No population estimate is given.

1 Maccabees 2:1, 15-28: Mattathias the priest 'moved from Jerusalem and settled in Modein'; royal officers came 'to the town of Modein' to make its people sacrifice; a Jew offered sacrifice 'on the altar in Modein'; Mattathias killed him and the officer, 'cried out in the town' and fled with his sons, leaving 'all that they had in the town'. Outbreak of the Maccabean revolt (c. 167 BCE). Documents a Judean town community (residents, Hasmonean family); no figure.

Josephus, Antiquities 12.265, 268 (Whiston): Mattathias 'dwelt at Modin'; the king's officers 'were come to Modin' to compel the inhabitants to sacrifice (outbreak of the revolt, c. 167 BCE). Ancient literary attestation of Jewish residents; no figure.

1 Maccabees 2:70: Mattathias died and 'was buried in the tomb of his ancestors at Modein' (Seleucid year 146 = 166/165 BCE). Ancestral family tomb indicates the Hasmonean family's long-standing ties to the town.
1 Maccabees 9:19: Jonathan and Simon buried Judas Maccabaeus 'in the tomb of their ancestors at Modein' after his death at Elasa (c. 160 BCE). Continued Hasmonean family tomb at Modein.

Earliest hall (c. 3.8 x 7.0 m) beneath the synagogue at Kh. Umm el-'Umdan, probably Seleucid period (2nd c. BCE; midpoint -150); six Seleucid coins of Antiochus III and Antiochus IV on its floors (IAA excavation 2013, Weksler-Bdolah, Hadashot Arkheologiyot 126). Earliest building phase of the (later Jewish) village; whether this first hall was already a synagogue is uncertain.

Encyclopaedia Judaica (Modi'in): Modi'in lay in the toparchy of Lydda; under Jonathan it passed into Jewish (Hasmonean) possession together with the rest of the Lydda toparchy (Lydda toparchy transferred to Judea c. 145 BCE; c.). Event: political incorporation into Hasmonean Judea. No population figure in the article.

1 Maccabees 13:25-30: Simon brought the bones of Jonathan and 'buried him in Modein, the city of his ancestors'; built a high monument over the tomb of his father and brothers with seven pyramids, great columns, armor and carved ships - 'This is the tomb that he built in Modein; it remains to this day.' Jonathan died 143/142 BCE (c.). Monumental Hasmonean family mausoleum at Modein.

Josephus, Antiquities 13.210-212 (Marcus): Simon buried Jonathan 'in Modeei, his birthplace', and built for his father and brothers a great monument of polished white marble with porticoes, monolithic pillars and seven pyramids, which 'have been preserved to this day' (i.e. still standing in Josephus' time, late 1st c. CE). c. 143 BCE. Confirms Modein as the Hasmonean brothers' birthplace.

Hasmonean-period Jewish agricultural estate excavated by the IAA (A. Tendler) on a hill in the modern city of Modi'in (a separate site, not necessarily ancient Modein): 'a Jewish family established an agricultural estate on this hill during the Hasmonean period'; a hoard of silver coins 'dating to the Hasmonean Period (126 B.C.E.)' (tetradrachms of Antiochus VII and Demetrius II) hidden in a rock fissure, a mikveh and winepresses. Presence of one Jewish family household; no figure.

Hasmonean synagogue at Kh. Umm el-'Umdan: a larger hall (c. 6.7 x 10.5-11.5 m) with benches on three sides built over the earlier hall; dated by five Hasmonean coins of John Hyrcanus and Alexander Jannaeus and Hellenistic-Hasmonean pottery; wall paintings of the 1st c. BCE. Dated to the Hasmonean period (end 2nd-1st c. BCE; Hasmonean midpoint -90 per brief). Communal building of a Jewish village; no population figure.

IAA rescue excavation 2002 east of Kh. Umm el-'Umdan (Onn & Weksler-Bdolah, Hadashot Arkheologiyot 118): three burial systems, quarries, a cistern and an ancient road linked to the rural Second Temple settlement; pottery of the Hasmonean and Herodian periods, 'mainly from the 1st c. BCE' (midpoint -50); Tomb 1 (compared with Jason's Tomb in Jerusalem) used mainly in the Hasmonean period until ossuaries came into use; the Hellenistic and Early Roman periods described as the settlement's floruit. Jewish burial practice of the village population; no figure.

Herodian synagogue at Kh. Umm el-'Umdan: a new, wider hall (c. 8.6 x 10.5-11.5 m) with 2-3 tiered benches on all four walls and two rows of four columns; benches dated to the Herodian period, most likely the second half of the 1st c. BCE (Herodian midpoint -20); a Hasmonean palm-branch coin (129-76 BCE) in the bench core. One of the few Second Temple synagogues known; village community; no figure.

Prof. Yoel Elitzur (kipa.co.il, chapter of his book 'Maqom ba-Parasha'): at Kh. el-Hammam (formerly Kh. el-Midya), the alternative candidate for ancient Modi'in near the 'Tombs of the Maccabees', there are 'typical Jewish burial caves with ossuaries' at the foot of the ruin; at Kh. Umm el-'Umdan a settlement existed 'mainly in the Hellenistic and Hasmonean period and until the Bar Kokhba revolt'. Ossuaries are undated in the source; Early Roman period midpoint used (4; c.). Presence of Jewish families at the rival Modi'in candidate site; no figure.

Mikveh (building 4) of two rock-cut subterranean rooms built west of the synagogue at Kh. Umm el-'Umdan in the first half of the 1st c. CE (midpoint 25; c.). Aramaic inscriptions incl. a seal on a stone 'measuring cup' handle with a four-letter inscription 'in a crude Jewish script' (read by J. Naveh as 'vinegar'). Evidence of Jewish ritual practice of the residents; no figure.

Violent destruction at Kh. Umm el-'Umdan: 'signs of a violent destruction, as in ash layers in the synagogue'; coins of Year 2 and Year 3 of the First Jewish Revolt in the debris; a coin of Nero of 68 CE in the plaster floor sealing the destruction shows it occurred before 68 CE; the excavators link it to the campaign of Cestius Gallus at the end of 66 CE (c.; note the tension with the Year 2-3 revolt coins). Event: destruction during the Great Revolt; not 0 because the Jewish inhabitants stayed and repaired the village.

Prof. Boaz Zissu (Bar-Ilan Univ.), quoted in ynet: the public building at Kh. Umm el-'Umdan, identified by excavators A. Onn and S. Weksler-Bdolah as probably a synagogue, 'served the Jewish village for about a hundred years - until its end in the Great Revolt'; after the revolt the synagogue was restored and functioned until its final destruction in the Bar Kokhba revolt. Zissu calls it the oldest synagogue in the Land of Israel. Year = Great Revolt 66 (c.). No population figure.

Hasmonean-period Jewish estate in modern Modi'in (IAA, A. Tendler; separate site): coins of 'Year Two' of the First Jewish Revolt with the legend 'Freedom of Zion' found on the estate (the article gives 66 C.E.; Year Two = 67/68 CE). Continued Jewish occupation of the estate during the Great Revolt; no figure.

Kh. Umm el-'Umdan after the destruction: a new plaster floor with a coin of Nero of 68 CE sealed the destruction level in the synagogue hall; 'This swift repair of the ruins was presumably carried out by the Jewish inhabitants of the village' during the First Revolt; the village was occupied at least until the Second Jewish Revolt (Year 2 Bar Kokhba coin near the mikveh). Continuity of the Jewish village through 70 CE; no figure.
